title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
story_key: Anthropic: FlashProve zkSNARK provable inference prototype
summary: Anthropic researchers present FlashProve, an open-source system based on zero-knowledge succinct proofs (zkSNARKs) that would let a model provider commit to a model and prove each response came from it, without revealing the weights. Their benchmark on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B mixture-of-experts model, 4-bit quantized) reports about 110 tokens/second per H100 GPU, roughly 19 MB of proof per 1,024-token request, and about 70-95x the GPU time of running the model on vLLM. They also release a fast C++ verifier and Lean formal proofs of the top-level security claims. The figures are the authors' own and not yet independently replicated, and they describe the work as intermediate progress.
why_it_matters: If you route LLM calls through third parties or need to verify which model served a response, this points to a future option, but at the current overhead it is a research prototype rather than something to adopt within months.

title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
story_key: Claude Platform: message threads public beta
summary: Anthropic has released message threads in public beta on the Claude Platform. With a thread, agents send only new messages and the previous response ID each turn instead of resending the full conversation, which the post says cuts time to first token for long sessions. The post reports a median TTFT drop of about 35% for requests of 500k to 1M tokens in Claude Code, where the feature is on by default for most users. Token usage stays the same because Claude still reads the full conversation each turn, and a thread expires 5 minutes after its last request.
why_it_matters: If I build long-running Claude agents, I can cut latency by threading requests instead of resending full histories, though I need to plan for the 5-minute expiry and the unchanged token cost.

why_it_matters: If you rely on LLMs to follow evolving state across long documents or chained updates, this suggests you should test those pipelines on long inputs rather than assume reliable tracking, and the architecture findings are a long-term signal for model choice.

title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
story_key: Route Anything: model and policy routing study across general-purpose AI systems
summary: The authors built a test set of 374,401 scored runs from 452 model and policy configurations across 25 benchmarks (language, image, video, speech, coding agents, and robot manipulation). Per-input oracle routing beats the best single fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers beat it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks. The paper reports 8.82x average efficiency gains over a reference model, but the text does not explain how that figure was measured. This is a single arXiv preprint with moderate early attention (87 upvotes), so treat the numbers as a lab's claims until others reproduce them.
why_it_matters: If you build with LLMs such as Claude, it suggests that routing requests across models by cost and quality is a practical lever for lowering spend, though the learned-router gains here are modest and the benefit is a medium-term design consideration rather than an immediate change.

title: Snowflake CoWork Adds Profiles, Dashboards & Automations
story_key: Snowflake CoWork: Profiles, Dashboards and Automations
summary: Snowflake announced new CoWork capabilities: Profiles, which route user questions to the right agent without the user choosing one, and Snowflake Dashboards (public preview), which the agent can discuss and query against the governed data behind them. Automations run recurring tasks on a schedule using the user's own permissions, and some can take actions such as creating a Jira ticket or sending a Slack message. Most of the other capabilities are generally available, and Cortex AI Gateway for model access governance is in public preview. The announcement is vendor-written and the Dashboard feature is still in preview.
why_it_matters: It shows a competing BI platform moving toward conversational, agent-driven dashboards on governed data, a direction Fabric and Power BI will be measured against, though it does not change anything I can use today.

title: Snowflake CoCo: Autonomous Cloud Agents for Data Work
story_key: Snowflake CoCo: autonomous Cloud Agents, automations and Cortex Agent SDK GA
summary: Snowflake announced updates to its CoCo agent: Cloud Agents that keep running long sessions after the user leaves, plus automations that run recurring jobs on a schedule or webhook under the creator's permissions. Several pieces are stated as generally available (skills and plugin sharing, the Cortex Agent SDK in Python and TypeScript) while memory, dynamic model routing and MCP connector management via Cortex AI Gateway Tools are in public preview. The post is largely promotional and includes no independent benchmarks or customer evidence.
why_it_matters: For someone building LLM agents, the GA Cortex Agent SDK and the scheduled-automation pattern are a concrete reference for running unattended agent work, though this only matters directly if Snowflake is in your stack.

title: Business Ontology: Governed Context for AI | Snowflake
story_key: Snowflake announces Business Ontology (public preview soon)
summary: Snowflake announced Business Ontology, a governance layer in Horizon Context where teams define business concepts, metrics and their relationships, with owners and approval status, linked to the semantic views and tables that implement them. Only approved definitions are served to AI agents in CoCo and CoWork, and definitions can be imported and exported via open formats (Apache Ossie, RDF). The feature is announced as public preview 'soon', and much of the text is vendor positioning and partner quotes.
why_it_matters: For a Fabric and Power BI shop building LLM agents, it signals that business definitions may increasingly live in a governed, shared layer separate from any single semantic model, which is worth tracking against your own semantic model and metric governance design.

title: Governed Context, Security and Spend Controls for AI Agents | Snowflake
story_key: Snowflake: AI agent governance, FinOps and Business Ontology update
summary: Snowflake's product page bundles several features: per-user and org-level budgets and quotas (GA), tag-based cost anomaly detection (GA), Optima automatic clustering key selection (GA), and Business Ontology (public preview soon). It also describes Cortex AI Gateway and agent observability, with several items in private preview. Most of the text is positioning for Snowflake's own platform.
why_it_matters: Snowflake's agent cost controls and governance layer are relevant only if you run Snowflake alongside Fabric, and the page does not change anything for a Fabric/Power BI stack.
exclusion_reason: marketing or case study: vendor product marketing bundling several minor features; no new information for a Fabric/Power BI reader

title: Real-Time Analytics on Snowflake: Stream, Transform, Serve
story_key: Snowflake: real-time analytics bundle (Interactive Analytics, streaming transformations, Datastream)
summary: Snowflake presents a combined real-time stack covering ingestion, in-flight transformation and serving on native and Iceberg tables. Zero-Copy Interactive is described as generally available, while streaming transformations and Datastream are in private preview. Performance and cost figures are vendor-reported internal tests and a McKnight Consulting Group benchmark commissioned by Snowflake, so they should be treated as claims rather than independent results.
why_it_matters: For a Fabric and Power BI shop it is a benchmark for how a competing platform packages real-time serving and in-stream transformation, useful when judging Fabric's real-time options, though the preview features are not yet usable in production.
